sections.content: During the Migration Period, several peoples lived at the same time in the Carpathian Basin, or in different parts of it. To express two simultaneous events in one sentence, you use the conjunction *míg*: "while" — two things happening at the same time. A *míg*-clause can stand at the start or the end of the sentence.

sections.title: míg — simultaneity
rows: while ... (both clauses are in the same tense)

items.spanish: Míg a rómaiak Pannóniában uralkodtak, a medence keleti részén más népek éltek.
items.english: While the Romans ruled in Pannonia, other peoples lived in the eastern part of the basin.

items.spanish: Az avarok uralták a medence nagy részét, míg a szlávok fokozatosan tovább terjeszkedtek.
items.english: The Avars ruled most of the basin, while the Slavs gradually kept expanding.

items.spanish: Míg egyes népek csak átvonultak a Kárpát-medencén, mások hosszabb időre letelepedtek.
items.english: While some peoples merely passed through the Carpathian Basin, others settled for a longer time.

sections.content: *míg* has two meanings: "while" (two things happen at once) and "until" (one thing continues until something else changes it). If both clauses describe an ongoing, simultaneous action in the same tense, *míg* generally means "while". The word *addig* is optional, but it reinforces the contrast. *miközben* ("while, as") also joins two simultaneous actions: *Erős lovas birodalmat alapítottak, miközben szláv csoportok telepedtek le a folyók mentén* (from this lesson's story).
